title: As... as
goal: Student compares equality (as + adj + as), inequality (not as + adj + as), multiplied quantities (twice/three times as + adj + as), and parallel progression (the more X, the more Y).
connects_to: M10 (Zero conditional) — after refining comparisons, move to general truths.
module_chunks: as + adjective + as (as tall as / as fast as)
not as + adjective + as (not as cold as)
twice as + adj + as / three times as + adj + as
the more X, the more Y (parallel structures)
as much as / as many as (uncountable / countable)
nearly / almost / nowhere near as + adj + as (degrees)

units.title: As tall as
units.grammar_focus: as + adjective + as (equality between two things)
units.real_life_context: You compare two people, places, or things as being equal in some quality.

grammar.sentence: My brother is _____ tall _____ my father.
grammar.explanation: For equality, use "as + adjective + as": "as tall as". Note that "so...as" is archaic in affirmative sentences — only "as...as" works in modern English.

grammar.sentence: This coffee is _____ strong _____ the one I had yesterday.
grammar.explanation: "As strong as" — direct equality comparison. Works with any descriptive adjective (strong, fast, easy, expensive).

grammar.sentence: It's _____ in São Paulo today.
grammar.explanation: "As + adjective + as" structure for geographic comparison. Always two "as" — one before and one after the adjective.

grammar.sentence: My new laptop is _____ my old one.
grammar.explanation: Equality comparison between two objects. "As fast as" is the standard form.

grammar.sentence: She runs _____ fast _____ her older brother.
grammar.explanation: "As fast as" — equality of speed between two people. Both "as" are required.

grammar.sentence: The exam was _____ difficult _____ I expected.
grammar.explanation: "As difficult as I expected" — confirming expectation. Common with expectation verbs (expected, thought, imagined).

grammar.sentence: He works _____ hard _____ anyone in the office.
grammar.explanation: "As hard as anyone" — used to highlight a maximum. "Anyone" implies no one surpasses it.

grammar.sentence: She's so beautiful as her sister.
grammar.hint: For equality in modern English, use as...as (not so...as)
grammar.answer: She's as beautiful as her sister.
grammar.explanation: "So...as" only appears in negatives/questions in very formal English. For affirmatives, always use "as...as".

grammar.sentence: He's tall as his father.
grammar.answer: He's as tall as his father.
grammar.explanation: The "as...as" structure always has TWO "as" — one before the adjective and one after. Forgetting the first one is a common mistake.

grammar.passage: My brother is as tall as my father — both are six feet. My sister is as smart as our mother. The new restaurant is as expensive as the old one — both are pricey but worth it.
grammar.question: How does the new restaurant compare to the old one?
grammar.answer: as expensive as the old one (or "equally expensive")
grammar.explanation: The text says "The new restaurant is as expensive as the old one" — both are equally expensive.

listening_speaking.text: My brother is as tall as my father.
This coffee is as strong as yesterday's.
She runs as fast as her brother.
It's as hot as Rio today.
The exam was as difficult as I expected.

units.title: Not as...as
units.grammar_focus: not as + adjective + as (expressing inequality, "less than")
units.real_life_context: You express that something is less than another in some quality — softer than "X is more Y than Z".

grammar.sentence: Today isn't _____ hot _____ yesterday.
grammar.explanation: "Not as + adj + as" = less than. Equivalent to "less hot than" but more natural in speech. Both "as" are still required.

grammar.sentence: My new job _____ as stressful as the old one.
grammar.explanation: The negation goes on the verb "to be" before "as". "Isn't as stressful as" = is less stressful than.

grammar.sentence: This book isn't _____ the last one.
grammar.explanation: "Not as good as" — negative comparison. Note: "isn't as good as" means INFERIOR to the other.

grammar.sentence: She _____ as tall as her sister.
grammar.explanation: Negation of "to be": "isn't" before "as tall as".

grammar.sentence: The movie wasn't _____ exciting _____ the book.
grammar.explanation: "Not as exciting as" — common in film-adaptation comparisons. The movie is less enjoyable than the book.

grammar.sentence: I'm not _____ patient _____ my mother.
grammar.explanation: "Not as patient as" — admitting a lesser quality in oneself. A common way to indirectly compliment someone else.

grammar.sentence: This restaurant _____ as expensive as the one downtown.
grammar.explanation: "Isn't as expensive as" — lower price than another option.

grammar.sentence: It isn't so hot as yesterday.
grammar.hint: Em inglês moderno, use "as...as" mesmo em negativa
grammar.answer: It isn't as hot as yesterday.
grammar.explanation: Although "so...as" still appears in older formal texts, standard modern English uses "not as...as" in both affirmative and negative.

grammar.sentence: She doesn't as smart as her brother.
grammar.hint: Negação do verbo to be, não usa "doesn't"
grammar.answer: She isn't as smart as her brother.
grammar.explanation: When the main verb is "to be", the negative uses "isn't/aren't", not "doesn't/don't". "She isn't as smart as her brother".

grammar.passage: My new apartment isn't as big as the old one, but it isn't as expensive either. The neighborhood isn't as quiet, but it isn't as far from work. Overall, it's a fair trade.
grammar.question: How does the new apartment compare to the old one in size?
grammar.explanation: The text says "My new apartment isn't as big as the old one" — meaning the new one is smaller.

listening_speaking.text: Today isn't as hot as yesterday.
My new job isn't as stressful as the old one.
This book isn't as good as the last one.
I'm not as patient as my mother.
It isn't as cold as I expected.

units.title: Twice as much
units.real_life_context: You compare with multiplied or divided quantities — emphasizing scale.

grammar.sentence: He's _____ as fast _____ I am.
grammar.explanation: "Twice as + adj + as" = 2x more. "Twice" is the idiomatic choice over "two times" in comparisons.

grammar.sentence: This trip costs _____ as much _____ the last one.
grammar.explanation: From 3x onward, use "three/four/five times as + adj + as". "Twice" is the exception ("two times" isn't used in comparisons).

grammar.sentence: She earns _____ I do.
grammar.explanation: "Twice as much as" — doubled quantity. Note the full structure: twice + as much + as.

grammar.sentence: We have _____ guests this year.
grammar.explanation: "Twice as many" for countables (guests, people, books). "Twice as much" for uncountables (money, time, water).

grammar.sentence: He works _____ as hard _____ his colleague.
grammar.explanation: "Twice as hard as" — doubled effort. "Twice" always before "as".

grammar.sentence: This apartment is _____ times as expensive _____ the other.
grammar.explanation: Multipliers of 3+ use "X times as + adj + as".

grammar.sentence: She spent _____ as much time on this project _____ I did.
grammar.explanation: "Twice as much time as" — time is uncountable, so "much".

grammar.sentence: He's two times faster as me.
grammar.answer: He's twice as fast as me.
grammar.explanation: "Two times faster as" combines two errors: it should be "twice" (not "two times" in comparisons) and "as...as" (not "faster as").

grammar.sentence: It costs three times more as that.
grammar.hint: Estrutura é "X times as + adj + as", não "X times more as"
grammar.answer: It costs three times as much as that.
grammar.explanation: "Three times more" + "as" don't combine. The correct structure is "three times as + much/many + as".

grammar.passage: She works twice as hard as I do — putting in extra hours daily. Her salary is also twice as much. This year, we have three times as many clients as last year — business is booming.
grammar.question: How many more clients does the company have this year?
grammar.answer: three times as many (or "three times more")
grammar.explanation: The text says "we have three times as many clients as last year".

listening_speaking.text: He's twice as fast as I am.
This trip costs three times as much.
She earns twice as much as I do.
We have twice as many guests this year.
She works twice as hard.

units.title: The more, the better
units.grammar_focus: Parallel comparatives — "the more X, the more Y"
units.real_life_context: You express how two things increase or decrease together — cause-effect with intensity.

grammar.sentence: _____ more I study, _____ better I understand.
grammar.explanation: The parallel structure "the more X, the more Y" requires "the" before both comparatives. It signals simultaneous progression: the more X, the more Y.

grammar.sentence: The harder you work, _____ you achieve.
grammar.explanation: Second half of the parallel structure. "The more" can appear with any noun (the more money, the more friends).

grammar.sentence: The colder it gets, _____.
choices: the more I want hot chocolate
grammar.answer: the more I want hot chocolate
grammar.explanation: The second clause follows normal order: "the more + subject + verb + complement". Don't invert.

grammar.sentence: The older I get, _____ family means to me.
grammar.explanation: "The more" works as an adverb modifying the verb "means". The more years, the more importance.

grammar.sentence: _____ harder you practice, _____ better you become.
grammar.hint: estrutura paralela the + comparativo, the + comparativo
grammar.explanation: "The harder, the better" — short -er comparatives also follow the parallel pattern. Harder practice = better outcome.

grammar.sentence: The sooner you start, _____ sooner you finish.
grammar.explanation: "The sooner...the sooner" — repeating the same comparative is common in advice.

grammar.sentence: The less I worry, _____ happier I feel.
grammar.explanation: "The less" also works — you can mix "less" on one side and "more/happier" on the other. The parallel structure is flexible.

grammar.sentence: More you study, more you learn.
grammar.hint: estrutura paralela precisa de "the" duas vezes
grammar.answer: The more you study, the more you learn.
grammar.explanation: Without "the", the sentence is grammatically incomplete — the most common error in parallel comparatives.

grammar.sentence: The more harder I try, the more better the result.
grammar.answer: The harder I try, the better the result.
grammar.explanation: "Harder" and "better" are already comparatives. "More harder" and "more better" are redundant — the direct comparative is enough.

grammar.passage: The more I learn English, the more confident I feel. The harder I practice speaking, the more naturally it comes. The older I get, the more I appreciate good conversations.
grammar.question: What happens when the speaker practices speaking harder?
grammar.answer: it comes more naturally (or "the more naturally it comes")
grammar.explanation: The text says "the harder I practice speaking, the more naturally it comes".

listening_speaking.text: The more I study, the better I understand.
The harder you work, the more you achieve.
The older I get, the more I appreciate family.
The colder it gets, the more I want hot chocolate.
The sooner, the better.

units.title: All comparisons combined
units.real_life_context: You combine all comparison forms in one description, choosing the right structure for each idea.

grammar.sentence: He's _____ tall _____ his brother — both are 1m80.
grammar.explanation: For exact equality, "as + adj + as". The context "both are 1m80" confirms equality.

grammar.sentence: Today _____ as cold _____ yesterday.
grammar.explanation: "Isn't as cold as" — negative inequality. Negative "to be" + as...as structure.

grammar.sentence: She earns _____ I do.
grammar.explanation: Multiplier "twice" + "as much as" (uncountable money). Other forms are incorrect.

grammar.sentence: _____ more I practice, _____ better I get.
grammar.explanation: Parallel structure: "The more...the better" — always "the" before the comparatives.

grammar.sentence: It's _____ as easy as it looks.
grammar.explanation: "Not as easy as it looks" — common phrase to signal real difficulty.

grammar.sentence: This trip cost _____ as much _____ the last one.
grammar.explanation: "Three times as much as" — multiplier + "as much as".

grammar.sentence: _____ harder you try, _____ more you accomplish.
grammar.explanation: "The harder, the more" — parallel structure with a short comparative.

grammar.sentence: He's so tall as me.
grammar.hint: inglês moderno usa as...as em afirmativas
grammar.explanation: "So...as" is archaic in affirmatives — always use "as...as".

grammar.sentence: She earns two times more as I do.
grammar.answer: She earns twice as much as I do.
grammar.explanation: "Twice as much as" — "two times more as" combines two errors (use "twice" and "as much as").

grammar.passage: My new apartment is as big as the old one, but it's not as quiet. The rent is twice as expensive, but the location is amazing. The more I live here, the more I appreciate the convenience.
grammar.question: How much more does the rent cost?
grammar.explanation: The text says "The rent is twice as expensive" — meaning the rent is doubled.

listening_speaking.text: He's as tall as me, but not as strong.
She earns twice as much as I do.

guided_chat.suggested_script:
**Script** (referencial, 7 turnos):

1. **Charlotte**: "Modern life isn't as simple as before, but it's not all bad. What do you think?"
2. **Student**: "Modern life isn't as peaceful as before."
3. **Charlotte**: "True — constant input. Any multipliers?"
4. **Student**: "We're twice as connected but not always closer."
5. **Charlotte**: "Sharp observation."
6. **Student**: "How about you?"
7. **Charlotte**: "The more options we have, the harder it is to choose. Modern vs past explored!"
